Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
A main methodological issue is the dose titration of tDCS. The dosage was set at 0.1 mA below skin perception threshold, up to a maximum of 2 mA (0.7-2 mA). This is an absolutely unusual, currents finally entering the brain vary almost 3 fold. They should of course correlate with intensity but the individual skin perception with individual current flow not. Current flow calculations e.g. with SIMNibs will be appreciated.
We thank the reviewer for this comment. We respectfully point towards other examples of highly varied transcranial electric stimulation titration. Pilloni et al used between 1.5 or 2.5 mA based on subject tolerability2. Simpson et al delivered between 1.0 – 1.5 mA based on subject tolerability3. Lafon et al delivered currents varying between 0.3 and 2 mA4. We also note there have also been numerous reports of no meaningful differences in outcomes from using different tDCS amperages5–7.
Perhaps more important, our study design is a cross-over experimental design, which looks at changes in the brain response within subjects. For each subject, the tDCS dose was held constant. Our results show, despite varying levels of initial scalp current, there is a significant increase in brain response for the tEAS conditions compared to others.
Nevertheless, we have run the requested simulations to estimate cortical current density. They are provided in Supplemental Table T1. Analysis of both scalp-level current and cortical current density do not show current intensity to be a meaningful (linear) predictor of the subjects’ tEAS response levels (all R2 < 0.05, all p > 0.05), which is consistent with the past studies reporting little-to-no differences from currents in our range5–7.
Supplemental Figure S7d and S7e: Mean tEAS-induced ROI activity is not well predicted by tDCS intensity. The tEAS cortical responses were fit with an affine function of tDCS scalp current and the cortical current density (estimated with SimNIBS). Neither of these hold meaningful predictive power for the tEAS responses (both p > 0.05, both R2 < 0.05).
We also performed a follow-up experiment with a 7-day washout out between etFUS and etEAS conditions. As part of this study, we used a consistent 0.7 mA of tDCS in the tEAS conditions for all subjects. The results were consistent with the main study, in which tEAS led to strong ROI activity while tFUS alone did not (Supplemental Figure S12).
We have added discussion the following manuscript (page 20):
“We note the varied level of scalp current applied to subjects during our experiments. There are, broadly, two approaches to transcranial electric stimulation dose determination for human experiments. One is to normalize the dose for all subjects (either at the scalp- or the cortical-level using simulations). The other is to use a varied dose across subjects2–4. We opted for the latter approach in our study for two reasons. The first reason is that we wanted to prioritize subject comfort and safety. tDCS is generally considered safe, and the scalp sensations of tingling, itching, and/or burning are often reported as transient8. However, it is possible for tDCS to induce skin lesions after only a single session9. Since our participants were healthy human subjects, we wanted to avoid this possibility. The second reason is that skin perceptions are the result of activated sensory neurons10, which can contaminate the resting-state EEG recordings, both from the firing of the scalp (i.e., non-cortical) neurons, but also from the activated pain circuits within the brain itself. We wished to avoid such possible contamination.
Since we used the same current density for each condition within a subject, the varied current density across subjects is not a major concern. This is because our cross-over study design looks at the changes in brain response across conditions for subjects.
Our results show a significant increase in ROI activity for tEAS conditions, regardless of initial tDCS dosage. We did conduct further analysis to determine if scalp or cortical (estimated with SIMNibs simulations11) tDCS dose (Supplemental Table T1) was a meaningful predictor of ROI response. Our results indicate tDCS dose, at the between-subjects level, is not a meaningful predictor of tEAS activation (Supplemental Figure S7; R2 < 0.05, p < 0.05). This is consistent with other studies that have reported little-to-no differences in the outcomes of different tDCS doses5–7, and further supports that our subject-specific dosage should not be viewed as a study limitation. In a follow-up study, we used a constant 0.7 mA tDCS for all subjects and found a consistent activation pattern across subjects for the tEAS condition (Supplemental Figure S12).”
Supplemental Figure S12: Results of a 7-day washout experiment and constant 0.7 mA scalp current are consistent with the main study. We repeated our etEAS and etFUS resting state conditions in 8 subjects, this time with a 7-day washout period between the two conditions. For etEAS, we used a consistent 0.7 mA of current across all subjects. We also tested each condition twice; once before and once after a 5 minute break. a) The ROI activity for etFUS was not significantly altered pre/post break (two-tailed permutation t-test; p > 0.05), and Bayes Factor analysis reveals the activities to be robustly statistically similar for a range of scaling factors. b) The ROI activity for the etEAS condition was also statistically similar before and after the 5 minute break period. c) The induced sources are consistent with those from the main study.
For each condition the inter-trial interval was 2 seconds with up to a 20% (0.4 s) random jitter, so each condition lasting 6.6-8min. A five-minute break was taken between each condition to allow for the subjects to stretch and let any cumulative effects of neuromodulation dissipate. This is a rather short interval neglecting results in the literature suggesting e.g that 3 min or 20 min breaks boost plasticity and influence hereby succeeding stimulation results. The authors are of course welcome to come up with references that this is not of relevance here.
We thank the reviewer for the comment. We removed the comment about letting neuromodulation effects dissipate from our methods:
“For each condition the inter-trial interval was 2 seconds with up to a 20% (0.4 s) random jitter, so each condition lasting 6.6-8min. A five-minute break was taken between each condition to allow for the subjects to stretch.”
We have added the following discussion to our paper to indicate why our experimental design helps to mitigate confounding sequential effects. In our new 7-day washout follow up study, we also tested each condition twice before/after a 5 minute break. Our results found ROI activity pre and post 5-minute break to be statistically similar from each other, further supporting that our results were not confounded from these breaks (page 21).
We randomized the order of our experiments across subjects, which is also known as counterbalancing. While it is possible that conditions tested within a single session may experience a carry-over or sequence-based effect, counterbalancing, at the group-level, helps ensure that these effects were randomly distributed across conditions and should not confound the main results12. To further validate our main findings, we conducted an additional follow-up study, in which we repeated our etEAS and etFUS experiments with a 7-day wash out period (8 participants; split 50/50 for which condition was first). On the day the condition was tested, we tested it twice: once ‘pre’ 5-minute break and once ‘post’ break. The ROI activity for each condition was statistically similar before and after the break (Supplemental Figure S12a-b), suggesting that, even without the counterbalancing of the main study, the results may not have suffered from any sequential-based confounds. The source localizability of the experimental conditions were also consistent with the main study, where etEAS yielded strong targeting-location specific activity, and etFUS did not (Supplemental Figure S12c).
Supplemental Figure S12: Results of a 7-day washout experiment and constant 0.7 mA scalp current are consistent with the main study. We repeated our etEAS and etFUS resting state conditions in 8 subjects, this time with a 7-day washout period between the two conditions. For etEAS, we used a consistent 0.7 mA of current across all subjects. We also tested each condition twice; once before and once after a 5 minute break. a) The ROI activity for etFUS was not significantly altered pre/post break (two-tailed permutation t-test; p > 0.05), and Bayes Factor analysis reveals the activities to be robustly statistically similar for a range of scaling factors. b) The ROI activity for the etEAS condition was also statistically similar before and after the 5 minute break period. c) The induced sources are consistent with those from the main study.
3 kHz PRF tFUS under the right prefrontal cortex share a striking resemblance to tFUS applied under left motor cortex area (Left M1) with 10 – 63, 20 – 40, and 80 – 100 ms responses. Both cause a hemisphere-symmetric response, despite tFUS only being applied to one side. This needs explanation since seemingly this does not support evidence of a target-location specific effect. Also, Granger causality analysis of both itFUS and etFUS conditions shows significant increases in information flow from primary auditory cortex to the deep brain, and no changes in net information flow from the targeted ROI to the deep brain.
Thank you for your comment. We apologize that we were not clearer in our explanation of this phenomenon; this is critical evidence of tFUS’ subthreshold location-specific effect. In other words, when tFUS is applied by itself, we only see the whole brain auditory-based response, regardless of where tFUS is targeted. We have reworded our discussion to make this more clear.
Please see our revised paragraph below (bold added for emphasis) (page 14):
“Excitatory (3 kHz PRF) tFUS targeted to the left motor region, as part of etFUS, etEAS, and etDCS (which included a tFUS spatial control), induced distinct ERPs at approximately 30, 90, and 170 ms post stimulation onset (Figure 2a, Figure 4a). This is consistent with a previous study that identified V1-targeted tFUS induced EEG peaks, though their reported peak times were labeled as 55 ms, 100 ms, and 150 ms post sonication. However, when we compared these ERPs to those induced by applying tFUS to an entirely different brain region (right hemisphere prefrontal cortex), the resultant waveforms did not just lack statistical differences from each other—they were found to be statistically similar through Bayes Factor analysis (Figure 4b). These results provide critical evidence that location-specific effects of tFUS are subthreshold; by itself, tFUS produces the same responses regardless of where it is targeted.
Of course, these shared responses are time-locked event related potentials.
To put it another way, tFUS does induce a suprathreshold response. However, since the topology of these ERPs do not differ across targeting locations, they can be attributed to a whole brain auditory response. Indeed, the 3 kHz PRF EEG topographic spatial distributions of the 90 and 170 ms ERPs do share visual resemblance to the previously reported auditory induced N1 and P2 ERPs. Granger causality investigations, which revealed significantly increased A1 to deep brain information flow for both 30 Hz and 3 kHz tFUS conditions (Figure 4c), provide additional support that the ERPs are auditory related. Nevertheless, the present results that combining tFUS with tDCS led to spatially specific responses, when neither could do so individually (Figure 3), as well as itFUS dissociating the spectral connectivity between the ROI and the deep brain (Supplemental Figure S5), indicate that tFUS does have targeted-location specific effects.”
Even increased tFUS parameter (including duty cycle; higher pressure; sonication duration) continued to yield no changes in net information flow from the targeted ROI to the deep brain. Transcranial electro-acoustic stimulation（tEAS）under the left M1 produces a hemisphere specific exogenous ERPs（10-63ms，which is claimed to be driven by tDCS polarity, not the excitatory or inhibitory parameters of tFUS (but see tDCS comments above).
Thank you for your comments. The continued lack of differences between the tFUS-only conditions are all in support of a subthreshold modulatory effect. It is only when tFUS is combined with tDCS that we start to see location-specific information. We have added the following clarification to our discussion section (page 12):
“Analysis of the other parameters continued to show a lack of sonication-location specific suprathreshold responses, providing further support that tFUS’ location-specific effect is subthreshold (Figure 5).”
We have also added to our discussion on tDCS based on the above tDCS comments / analysis (bold added for emphasis) (page 12):
“Not only did itEAS and etEAS induce significantly higher source localization metrics and source power than the other tested conditions, but they also led to a significant change in ROI polarity (Figure 2d). While this polarity change is evidence of differing electrophysiological effects, a follow-up study indicates that this change in response is driven from tDCS polarity and not tFUS PRF (Supplemental Figure S7). However, further analysis shows no linear relationship between the applied tDCS dose and tEAS response magnitude (Supplemental Figure S7d-e), nor between tFUS intensity and tEAS response (Supplemental Figure S7c). This points to a non-linear response from a combined transcranial electro-acoustic effect.”
Anodal tDCS combined with 30Hz PRF tFUS (inhibitory) and 3,000 Hz (excitatory) PRF tFUS both led stronger ipsilateral than contralateral responses. But again, here tEAS conditions were also found to induce significant increases in auditory to deep brain connectivity without an effect on the net flow of information from the targeted ROI to deep brain.
Thank you for your comment. We have added the following statement to our discussion regarding tEAS and Granger causality (page 14-15):
“We note that these auditory effects persist within the tEAS conditions (Supplemental Figure S4). This is unsurprising, as we would have no reason to think the electro-acoustic effect at M1 would cancel out auditory pathways. However, what is surprising is the continued lack of ROI to deep brain change in net flow of information. M1 is connected to deep brain structures13, so on one hand it would be expected that increased M1 activity would lead to increased deep brain activity, and this would be reflected as an increased net flow of information. However, this was not our finding. One possible explanation for this phenomena is that M1 neuron connections with the deep brain are dependent on cell type13. Prior work has demonstrated tFUS’ parameter choices can alter cell-type selectivity14. Our tFUS parameters may not have been optimal for eliciting M1 to deep brain connections. Future research on tEAS connectivity changes (or lack thereof) are warranted.”
Why does tDCS applied under the left M1 synchronize the tFUS under the right frontal without causing local changes; instead, it still results in a hemisphere-symmetric response.
Our tDCS conditions are combined with a spatial-sham tFUS (Figure 1b). These hemisphere-symmetric responses are the continued results of auditory based effects from tFUS. We have clarified this point in the discussion (bold added for emphasis):
“Excitatory (3 kHz PRF) tFUS targeted to the left motor region, as part of etFUS, etEAS, and etDCS (which included a tFUS spatial control), induced distinct ERPs at approximately 30, 90, and 170 ms post stimulation onset (Figure 2a, Figure 4a).”
Is the claim that tEAS is more than a linear sum of its parts really supported by the summation of the source-space tFUS and tDCS conditions which in turn did not result in increased concordance with the ROI, nor to significant increases in ipsilateral under contralateral ROI source power.
Thank you for your comments. We have included linear modeling of tEAS source-space response as a function of tDCS / tFUS intensities (Supplemental Figure S7), which provide additional evidence of a non-linear response. We added the following line to the results section (page 10):
“We also modeled the tEAS ROI response as function of tDCS scalp current, cortical current, and tFUS intensity and found none of these component to be meaningfully predictive (Supplemental Figure S7c-e).”
Supplemental Figure S7: The transcranial electro-acoustic effect is more than just the summation of independent electric and acoustic modulation. a) Source-imaging data for itFUS and itDCS, as well as etFUS and tDCS, were added together for each subject, and then averaged across subjects. Visualizations continue to show strong off-targeted sources. b) The average ipsilateral ROI activity of the added sources continues to be not significantly greater than the contralateral ROI for both the summed excitatory and summed inhibitory conditions (p > 0.05). c – e) Mean tEAS-induced ROI activity is not well predicted by tFUS or tDCS intensity. None of the individual components hold meaningful predictive power for the tEAS responses (all p > 0.05).
So, in summary two main concerns regarding the tDCS intensity and intervals between different types of stimulation are worrying.
Thank you for your feedback. We have addressed these concerns with our updated analysis, discussion points, and follow-up study.
